My mind tires out fast; if I try to work on the accounts or plan the planting, my head feels drained within minutes and I just stare at the page.

I catch myself thinking a lot that it’d be easier if I just wasn’t here. I don’t have some big plan or anything, but the thought “what’s the point, maybe it’s better if I’m gone” keeps coming back.

Earlier this year there was a month where I was the complete opposite. I barely slept—maybe three, four hours—but woke up buzzing with energy, not tired at all. I’d rush from one task to another, pacing if I had nothing to do, fiddling with my hands, unable to sit still. My mood swung fast: one moment joking and feeling on top of the world, the next snapping at my wife over nothing. I talked so fast my family kept telling me to slow down, saying they couldn’t keep up. It didn’t really stop me working, but they were worried, said I wasn’t myself.

It’s kind of like I’ve been living in two completely different gears.

For most of this past year, I’ve felt…flat. Not sad in a crying way, just like everything’s muted. I go to the archive, I do what I have to do, but it feels like I’m moving through fog. Even reading old documents, which used to really absorb me, now wears me out quickly. My brain gets tired fast, like even basic cataloguing or cross‑checking is too much effort. Outside of work I mostly go straight home. I dodge messages, ignore invitations, let friendships fade because I just don’t have it in me to engage. It’s like I’m watching my own life from a distance. Sometimes, when I’m walking over a bridge or waiting near a busy road, I’ll get this sudden, almost physical urge to just step off or step out, even though I don’t have a plan or actually want to die. It scares me.

But about a month ago, everything suddenly flipped. I started feeling unbelievably good for no clear reason—energized, almost buzzing. I barely sleep now, maybe a couple of hours, but I don’t feel tired. At work I can’t sit still; I’m pacing between stacks, starting multiple projects at once, reorganizing things that don’t really need it. I talk nonstop to my coworkers, jumping from topic to topic, filling every silence because being quiet feels unbearable. My thoughts race ahead of my mouth. I’ve also been way more focused on sex than usual—constantly thinking about it, texting people late at night, hooking up more than I normally would. It feels exciting and “right” in the moment, but then I look back and wonder if I’m going too far. I’m still managing to show up and do my job, but I can tell something about the way I’m acting isn’t my normal.

It’s been a weird couple of years. The last nine months especially, I’ve felt like I’m running on empty all the time. I’m a trainer, so I’m used to being tired, but this is different—no matter how much I sleep, my body feels heavy, like I’m moving through water. Emotion‑wise, it’s like someone turned the volume way down. Clients tell me good news or bad news, and I just… don’t feel much. I go through the motions, but I’ve cut my hours because I can’t keep up. Between sets I just want to sit down, which isn’t like me at all.

Nights are rough. I’ll fall asleep okay, then wake up at 2 or 3 a.m. for no reason and stare at the ceiling, mind blank but restless, sometimes for hours.

But earlier this year, for about three weeks, it was the opposite. I was buzzing. I couldn’t sit still—if I wasn’t training clients, I was redesigning programs, planning an online course, talking about opening my own gym. I felt like I’d finally “figured it out,” like I was meant for something big, almost like I had this special role in helping people transform their lives. Little things set me off, though; if a client was late or questioned my routine, I’d snap way more than usual. I wasn’t totally falling apart or anything, I still worked, but everyone said I seemed “amped up” and on edge. Then it just kind of faded, and I slipped back into this dull, drained state.

I’m exhausted all the time, like I’ve done a double workout before I even get out of bed. Even on days I sleep early, I wake up two, three times a night and then just stare at the ceiling, unable to fall back asleep. The tiredness is really getting in the way of my work; I’ve cut back clients, and sometimes I cancel because I just can’t push through it.

A few months back, there was this three‑week stretch where I was the complete opposite. I was on edge, snapping at clients over tiny things, pacing around the gym because I couldn’t sit still. I took on way more classes and side projects than usual, convinced I was meant to be this elite, world‑changing coach. I honestly felt like I had some special purpose. D009-D008_h022.question_both:
It kind of feels like I’ve been living in two totally different gears.

For most of this past year, I’ve been dragging myself through the day. I’m a trainer, so I’m supposed to be the “motivator,” but I’ll just stare at my client list and feel no drive to do anything. Even routine stuff—writing programs, following up with clients—feels like climbing a mountain, and I put everything off. My brain gets tired so fast; if I’m trying to plan workouts or do any kind of paperwork, it’s like my mind just hits a wall and I have to stop. At the same time, I can’t sit still. I’ll pace around the gym, pick at my fingers, tap my feet nonstop, walk circles between the locker room and the front desk for no real reason. Emotionally, I feel kind of flat—like I’m watching my own life instead of feeling it. Good sessions, bad sessions, it all feels the same.

But then there was this stretch, a few months ago, where it flipped. I woke up feeling amazing—like everything was sharp and bright. I had all this energy, was insanely productive, taking on extra classes, redesigning the gym schedule, starting new side projects all at once. I’d stay up most of the night planning new programs or scrolling and messaging people about ideas, then show up to work after barely sleeping and still feel wired, like I didn’t even need rest. It didn’t really mess up my job—I was actually doing more than usual—but even when I went several nights with almost no sleep, I just kept going and didn’t feel tired or concerned about it. That “high” stretch gradually faded, and now I’m mostly back in that numb, restless, worn‑out place again.

I’d take on extra clients, redesign the whole gym schedule, start new training plans, and sign up for projects all at once. I was just “on,” talking fast, moving nonstop, but I was still able to do my job and didn’t do anything dangerous or out of control. I never felt out of touch with reality or heard or saw things.
